prompt_sources.name: Example: Identifying Linear Transformations
prompt_sources.problem:
Are the following transformations linear?
![](@asset-0@)
prompt_sources.worked_solution:
A linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ satisfies two properties:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}]=k\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}], \\  & \mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's consider $\mathbf{T}_1.$ Checking the first condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{T}}_{1}[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}(kx)^{2} \\ (kx)(ky)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{k}^{2}{x}^{2} \\ {k}^{2}xy\end{aligned}] \\  & =k[\begin{aligned}k{x}^{2} \\ kxy\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne k{\mathbf{T}}_{1}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\,{\color{red}\times }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\textbf{T}_1$ is not a linear transformation.

Now, let's consider $\mathbf{T}_2.$

- Checking the first condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{T}}_{2}[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3kx \\ kx+2ky\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}k(3x) \\ k(x+2y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =k[\begin{aligned}3x \\ x+2y\end{aligned}] \\  & =k{\mathbf{T}}_{2}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\,{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the second condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{T}}_{2}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\ ({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+2({y}_{1}+{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ ({x}_{1}+2{y}_{1})+({x}_{2}+2{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{1}+2{y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}+2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\mathbf{T}}_{2}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+{\mathbf{T}}_{2}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\,{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\textbf{T}_2$ is a linear transformation.

prompt_sources.problem:
Let 
$\mathbf{T}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ 2x+7y\end{aligned}].$
Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\mathbf{T}(k\mathbf{v})=k\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})$ for any real $2\times 1$ column vector $\mathbf{v}$ and real scalar $k$

II. $\mathbf{T}({\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2})=\mathbf{T}({\mathbf{v}}_{1})+\mathbf{T}({\mathbf{v}}_{2})$ for any real $2\times 1$ column vectors ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$

III. $\mathbf{T}$ is **NOT** a linear transformation

solution_sources.worked_solution:
A linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ satisfies two properties:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}]=k\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}], \\  & \mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the first condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}(kx)^{2}+(ky)^{2} \\ 2(kx)+7(ky)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{k}^{2}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) \\ k(2x+7y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =k[\begin{aligned}k({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) \\ 2x+7y\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne k\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\,{\color{red}\times }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\mathbf{\text{T}}$ is not a linear transformation.

- Checking the second condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})^{2}+({y}_{1}+{y}_{2})^{2} \\ 2({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+7({y}_{1}+{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}({x}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{1}^{2})+({x}_{2}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2})+2({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{y}_{1}{y}_{2}) \\ (2{x}_{1}+7{y}_{1})+(2{x}_{2}+7{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{1}^{2} \\ 2{x}_{1}+7{y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} \\ 2{x}_{2}+7{y}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{y}_{1}{y}_{2}) \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{y}_{1}{y}_{2}) \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne \mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\,{\color{red}\times }\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, only statement III is true.

\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}) \\ 2({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{y}_{1} \\ 2{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3{y}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\,{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\mathbf{\text{T}}$ is a linear transformation.

II. $\mathbf{T}({\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2})=\mathbf{T}({\mathbf{v}}_{1})+\mathbf{T}({\mathbf{v}}_{2})$ for any real $2\times 1$ column vectors ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
A linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ satisfies two properties:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}]=k\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}], \\  & \mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the first condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}kx+ky \\ 4kx+3ky\end{aligned}] \\  & =k[\begin{aligned}x+y \\ 4x+3y\end{aligned}] \\  & =k\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\,{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the second condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} \\ 4({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+3({y}_{1}+{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{y}_{1} \\ 4{x}_{1}+3{y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{y}_{2} \\ 4{x}_{2}+3{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\,{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\mathbf{\text{T}}$ is a linear transformation.

As a result, all three statements are true.

II. $\mathbf{T}({\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2})=\mathbf{T}({\mathbf{v}}_{1})+\mathbf{T}({\mathbf{v}}_{2})$ for any real $2\times 1$ column vectors ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
A linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ satisfies two properties:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}]=k\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}], \\  & \mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the first condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ kx\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne k\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\,{\color{red}\times }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\mathbf{\text{T}}$ is not a linear transformation.

- Checking the second condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ {x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne \mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+\mathbf{T}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\,{\color{red}\times }\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, only statement III is true.

solution_sources.worked_solution:
Since $\mathbf{T}$ is a linear transformation, it must satisfy $\mathbf{T}(k\mathbf{v})=k\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}).$ Noting that $[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -12\end{aligned}]=4[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}8 \\ -12\end{aligned}]) & =\mathbf{T}(4[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}])=4\mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since we're told that 

$$
\mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}8 \\ -12\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}16 \\ -20\end{aligned}],
$$

we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}4\mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]) & =[\begin{aligned}16 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\ \mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]) & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}16 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\ \mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]) & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
Since $\,\mathbf{T}\,$ is a linear transformation, it must satisfy $\,\mathbf{T}(k\mathbf{v})=k\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}).$ Noting that $[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 16\end{aligned}]=4[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}8 \\ 16\end{aligned}]) & =\mathbf{T}(4[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}])=4\mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since we're told that 

$$
\mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}8 \\ 16\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}28 \\ -20\end{aligned}],
$$

we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}4\mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]) & =[\begin{aligned}28 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\ \mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]) & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}28 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\ \mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]) & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
Since $\mathbf{T}$ is a linear transformation, it must satisfy $\mathbf{T}(k\mathbf{v})=k\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}).$ Noting that $[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 12\end{aligned}]=4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}4 \\ 12\end{aligned}]) & =\mathbf{T}(4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}])=4\mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since we're told that 

$$
\mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}4 \\ 12\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ 16\end{aligned}],
$$

we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}4\mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]) & =[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\ \mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]) & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\ \mathbf{T}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]) & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}17{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+12{\mathbf{v}}_{2} & =5{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+12{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+12{\mathbf{v}}_{2} \\  & =5{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+12({\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2}) \\  & =5{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+12(\mathbf{0}) \\  & =5{\mathbf{v}}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\mathbf{T}(17\mathbf{v}_1+12\mathbf{v}_2)=\mathbf{T}(5\mathbf{v}_1).
$$

Now, since $\mathbf{T}$ is a linear transformation, we have that $\mathbf{T}(k\mathbf{v})=k\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}).$ So 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}(5{\mathbf{v}}_{1}) & =5\mathbf{T}({\mathbf{v}}_{1}) \\  & =5[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -12 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}45 \\ -60 \\ 40\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
First, since ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0},$ we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}21{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+18{\mathbf{v}}_{2} & =18{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+3{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+18{\mathbf{v}}_{2} \\  & =18({\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2})+3{\mathbf{v}}_{1} \\  & =18(\mathbf{0})+3{\mathbf{v}}_{1} \\  & =3{\mathbf{v}}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\mathbf{T}(21{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+18{\mathbf{v}}_{2})=\mathbf{T}(3{\mathbf{v}}_{1}).
$$

Now, since $\mathbf{T}$ is a linear transformation, we have that $\mathbf{T}(k\mathbf{v})=k\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}).$ So 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}(3{\mathbf{v}}_{1}) & =3\mathbf{T}({\mathbf{v}}_{1}) \\  & =3[\begin{aligned}54 \\ -36 \\ 30\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}162 \\ -108 \\ 90\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, $\mathbf{T}(21{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+18{\mathbf{v}}_{2})=[\begin{aligned}162 \\ -108 \\ 90\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, we have

$$
\mathbf{T}(15{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+12{\mathbf{v}}_{2})=\mathbf{T}(3{\mathbf{v}}_{1}).

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}(3{\mathbf{v}}_{1}) & =3\mathbf{T}({\mathbf{v}}_{1}) \\  & =3[\begin{aligned}-25 \\ 16 \\ 20\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-75 \\ 48 \\ 60\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

In conclusion, $\mathbf{T}(15{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+12{\mathbf{v}}_{2})=[\begin{aligned}-75 \\ 48 \\ 60\end{aligned}].$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
First, since ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0},$ we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}7{\mathbf{v}}_{1}-5{\mathbf{v}}_{2} & =12{\mathbf{v}}_{1}-5{\mathbf{v}}_{1}-5{\mathbf{v}}_{2} \\  & =12{\mathbf{v}}_{1}-5({\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2}) \\  & =12{\mathbf{v}}_{1}-5(\mathbf{0}) \\  & =12{\mathbf{v}}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\mathbf{T}(7{\mathbf{v}}_{1}-5{\mathbf{v}}_{2})=\mathbf{T}(12{\mathbf{v}}_{1}).
$$

Now, since $\mathbf{T}$ is a linear transformation, we have that $\mathbf{T}(k\mathbf{v})=k\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}).$ So 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}(12{\mathbf{v}}_{1}) & =12\mathbf{T}({\mathbf{v}}_{1}) \\  & =12[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 24 \\ -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, $\mathbf{T}(7{\mathbf{v}}_{1}-5{\mathbf{v}}_{2})=[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 24 \\ -12\end{aligned}].$

prompt_sources.problem: Consider a linear transformation $\,\mathbf{T}\,.$ If $\,{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}\,$ and $\,\mathbf{T}({\mathbf{v}}_{1})=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 13 \\ -7\end{aligned}]\,$, find $\,\mathbf{T}(41{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+37{\mathbf{v}}_{2}).$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
First, since ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0},$ we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}41{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+37{\mathbf{v}}_{2} & =37{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+4{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+37{\mathbf{v}}_{2} \\  & =37({\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2})+4{\mathbf{v}}_{1} \\  & =37(\mathbf{0})+4{\mathbf{v}}_{1} \\  & =4{\mathbf{v}}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\mathbf{T}(41{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+37{\mathbf{v}}_{2})=\mathbf{T}(4{\mathbf{v}}_{1}).
$$

Now, since $\mathbf{T}$ is a linear transformation, we have that $\mathbf{T}(k\mathbf{v})=k\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}).$ So 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}(4{\mathbf{v}}_{1}) & =4\mathbf{T}({\mathbf{v}}_{1}) \\  & =4[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 13 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-16 \\ 52 \\ -28\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, $\mathbf{T}(41{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+37{\mathbf{v}}_{2})=[\begin{aligned}-16 \\ 52 \\ -28\end{aligned}].$

First, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}13{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+8{\mathbf{v}}_{2} & =13{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+13{\mathbf{v}}_{2}-5{\mathbf{v}}_{2} \\  & =13({\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2})-5{\mathbf{v}}_{2} \\  & =13(\mathbf{0})-5{\mathbf{v}}_{2} \\  & =-5{\mathbf{v}}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\mathbf{T}(13{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+8{\mathbf{v}}_{2})=\mathbf{T}(-5{\mathbf{v}}_{2}).
$$

 

Now, since $\mathbf{T}$ is a linear transformation, we have that $\mathbf{T}(k\mathbf{v})=k\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}).$ So 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}(-5{\mathbf{v}}_{2}) & =-5\mathbf{T}({\mathbf{v}}_{2}) \\  & =-5[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 4 \\ 9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}40 \\ -20 \\ -45\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, $\mathbf{T}(13{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+8{\mathbf{v}}_{2})=[\begin{aligned}40 \\ -20 \\ -45\end{aligned}].$

First, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}37{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+39{\mathbf{v}}_{2} & =37{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+37{\mathbf{v}}_{2}+2{\mathbf{v}}_{2} \\  & =37({\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2})+2{\mathbf{v}}_{2} \\  & =37(\mathbf{0})+2{\mathbf{v}}_{2} \\  & =2{\mathbf{v}}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\mathbf{T}(37{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+39{\mathbf{v}}_{2})=\mathbf{T}(2{\mathbf{v}}_{2}).
$$
